why: 'Presently closed' dropped from seasonal prose; closure restated as a dated fact without citing the NPS page

best_season.from: Both ends of the calendar have been used. The first ascent was in July, so the line goes as a summer rock-and-snow route; the only recorded winter ascent was 13 March 2005. Late winter through early spring is the more attractive window: the couloir is filled and frozen, the lower rock band takes hooks, thin ice and turf instead of being bare compact slab, the bergschrund is filled in, and the slide alder on the approach has no foliage. Against that, the snowpack must be settled — the whole route sits under the summit cornices — and the Stetattle Creek ford is unpleasant in any month. Consult the NWAC West Slopes North forecast before committing. Note that the approach trail is presently closed by fire damage regardless of season.

why: Dated 2001 anecdote and its quotation replaced with the hazard itself

from: Extremely loose rock, especially on the west side of #2 Gully. In 2001 a climber was struck and briefly pinned by a roughly 500-pound block that rolled out of the dirt near the base of the gully as he weighted it — he called it his closest call in the mountains and noted a broken leg up there could have meant a multi-day rescue.
Rockfall generated by your own party on the descent is the norm, not the exception; keep parties tight and helmets on.
Benightment is close to standard: twelve hours is an absolute minimum and documented ascents run past 11 p.m.
No reliable water above roughly 2,100 ft.
Wet conditions make the gully's mix of sand and polished rock unjustifiably dangerous.

why: Source-shaped wording ('beta on record') removed

best_season.from: Mid-July through mid-September is the realistic window. Earlier and the long Constance Pass approach still holds snow and the buttress ledges are iced or verglassed; later and autumn Pacific fronts return, which on this range means days of low cloud that make route-finding on the face impractical. The most stable spell is usually late July into August, when the Pacific high suppresses precipitation over the Olympics. Even then, plan around cloud rather than around rain — the most useful piece of beta on record is that cloud cover, as always in the Olympics, makes viewing the route very difficult.

beta.from: A January 2002 ascent recorded as 'Lichtenberg Mountain West Face 5.9+' was made by James Nakagami, climbing with Dan 'Danimal' Capellini and a third partner. The wall sits just above Lake Valhalla; the approach is a short walk from the Smithbrook trailhead of about an hour, and it is an easier walk in than Snow Creek Wall — the implicit pitch for the crag. A 'grand west face' is separately listed as one of the mountain's three distinct routes, and a party is on record as having been turned around by the sheer wall before eventually reaching the summit by an easier line, which corroborates that this is genuine roped terrain rather than a scramble. Beyond the grade, the location and the approach, the beta is thin: no topo, pitch count, rack list or descent description is available. Anyone going should expect to do their own reconnaissance from Lake Valhalla, and plan for a full trad rack and a walk-off.

why: Dated 2012 attempt and its quotation removed; the conditions it describes kept

best_season.from: Mid-July through August is the sweet spot: enough of the Borealis Glacier's snowpack remains to bridge crevasses solidly, but the approach trail is snow-free. By late September the glacier is largely bare and thin — a Sept. 2012 attempt found the standard east ridge 'nothing more than a walk' unavailable due to conditions at Lucky Pass, with bullet ice and loose rock instead.
best_season.to: Mid-July through August is the sweet spot: enough of the Borealis Glacier's snowpack remains to bridge crevasses solidly, but the approach trail is snow-free. By late September the glacier is largely bare and thin, and conditions at Lucky Pass can turn the normally easy east ridge into bullet ice and loose rock.

best_season.from: Trip reports favor mid-to-late summer through fall. An early-July ascent (July 2010) found lingering snow and a 'frigid summit,' so early season can still be wintry at this elevation. Multiple trip reports specifically recommend visiting around larch season (roughly late September) for more stable weather, drier talus, and better scenery; plan for the route to be most straightforward roughly August through October.
best_season.to: Mid-to-late summer through early fall is the favored window. Early July can still hold lingering snow and a frigid summit, so early season can be wintry at this elevation. Late September (larch season) often brings more stable weather, drier talus and better scenery; plan for the route to be most straightforward roughly August through September.

best_season.from: Most commonly climbed as a dry-season scramble from July through September, when the route is mostly snow-free talus and trail. It is also a popular spring snow climb in late April through May/early June, when consolidated snow fills the approach gullies and col, allowing efficient booting/step-kicking (crampons and ice axe recommended, especially for a firm-snow descent); trip reports from this window note 12-18 inches of soft snow over a firm base and cornice/slough hazard near the Rock Mountain col.
